Right now, there’s probably something you’re forgetting to do. Do you know what it is? Tech companies are wise to our absentmindedness, selling the solution back to us in the form of miced wearables that yearn to be our personal assistants.

Also: I tried the Flowtica Verso AI notetaker expecting a gimmick – now it’s my fresh favorite MagSafe gadget.

According to recent reports, over the past few weeks, I tested two such devices that claim to refresh my failing memory, but with very different approaches. One was Siri Recap, a beta feature on the latest Apple Watch that listens to your conversations and generates summaries. The other was the Pebble Index 01, a ring with a microphone and a button — and nothing else.

The two wearables illustrate how different companies are building the same product. The $75 Pebble Index 01 is open-source and easily integrated with plug-ins. Siri Recap is private and closed. The note-taking ring has one purpose. The Apple Watch has many. Consumers control what the Index 01 notes. Apple Watch users are at the whims of Siri. But which actually does the job better? I tested the Index 01 to see for myself.

Pebble’s Index 01 is not exactly a smart ring like the Oura Ring — it can’t track your heart rate or tell you how well you slept. Instead, it’s essentially a specialized mic with its own app, or a personalized agent, if that agent were wrapped around your finger. The ring comes in three colors: silver, gold, or black, and fits sizes six through 13. You can use it with or without an internet connection, and the Index 01 stores up to 5 minutes of recordings without your phone present.

Also: I watched a movie on Meta’s latest VR glasses – it was awesome, but isolating.

In a recent development, wearing the device felt like I was wearing another smart ring. While I didn’t sleep with it on, I definitely could have — and wouldn’t have noticed its presence. It was discreet and comfortable. It’s water-resistant, so I wore the ring while washing my hands and doing the dishes with no problems. It’s not rechargeable, with a battery life of around two to three years, depending on usage. Once it dies, you’ll have no choice but to buy another. Thankfully, $75 per ring isn’t a bad price.

Sources indicate that the Pebble Index 01 is a straightforward wearable. Have a stroke of genius or a grocery item you don’t want to forget? Press the button on the ring’s crown, and speak into the microphone. Your note will appear in the accompanying Pebble app, where it’s organized into shopping lists, to-dos, or customized lists.

I got a notification each time a note was recorded on the app, so I could quality-check my notes before they’re sorted, or redo any errors. The microphone didn’t pick up what was mentioned or misheard my note a few times, but these are easily editable within the app. Most of the time, the Index 01 works perfectly fine.

Recent findings suggest that the ring is designed to connect to various plugins, such as Claude Code, Muse, or Notion, so ring wearers can control where their queries go and use the device as a wearable agent. Because it’s so easy to connect to other apps, you can use the ring as if it’s an extension of your phone, asking the ring to turn on the smart lights through one app or vibe code a website in another. I connected my Index 01 to Claude, and sent it questions while my phone was out of reach.

In a recent development, I’ve found the ring to be most useful for the random stuff in my life. As I juggle work tasks, friends’ birthdays, holiday prepares, and my own growing list of to-dos, the Index 01 helped me to organize those fleeting moments where an important memory popped up I was too distracted to remember.

According to recent reports, the ring has helped me note important dates. It reminded me to ask my boyfriend about a DJ event I wanted to go to (I had even forgotten that I made that note in the first place). I’ve talked through my Saturday to-do list with the ring, organizing the list purely by voice. In fact, lists have become one of the main ways I’ve used the ring. The last list I added to consists of Christmas decorations and holiday outing ideas.

It has been revealed that one gripe is that you have to manually create fresh lists on the app. You can’t just make a new one verbally. I organize my to-do lists by date and keep separate lists for products I’ve been meaning to buy, as well as for notes to self and writing goals. These ideas are often stray thoughts I have one moment and forget the next, but the ring can capture and contain a single idea, holding me more accountable for my own creativity.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future.

Don’t get me wrong: I’m a pen-and-paper writer through and through, and won’t be ditching my physical agenda when it comes to organizing and time-stamping my to-do list. Nevertheless, the Index 01 assisted me when I didn’t have my notepad handy — or when I thought of something I’d need to remember in the distant future.

The bottom line? The ring has certainly helped me to remember more. Pebble accomplishes this, in part, by designing the technology to quickly organize and sort spoken notes. It also helps me to remember by simply forcing me to speak notes out loud — not just think them.

According to recent reports, after testing the Index 01, I’m less convinced that ambient-listening devices are the solution to the forgetfulness crisis. The Pebble Index 01 helped me remember better because I could speak to it directly, forcing me to take an active role in choosing what to note and prioritize. With the always-listening Siri Recap, I had far less control over what Siri deemed noteworthy enough to summarize.

Sources indicate that testing Siri Recap resulted in a lot of useless conversation summaries, listening for any voices at all without discernment. At one point, it even picked up on my TikTok scrolling and made a note on it. Another time, it summarized “Clubkid,” a movie I had watched with my friend, creating a note about drug addiction and child custody, as if I were the one experiencing these things and not the main character of the movie.

In a recent development, it was always listening. In doing so, it summarized information in the app that I had no use for, or made me sift through small talk to find a conversation tidbit I was looking for.

Also: I tested Siri Recap on my Apple Watch for a week – then turned it off, for good.

Industry observers note that tech companies are pushing all-seeing and all-listening devices at consumers left and right, but my time with the Index 01 proved to me that the best technology is rarely invasive. It can be as simple as a ring with a microphone and a helpful, accompanying app.

I’d recommend the Pebble Index 01 to anyone interested in a upcoming approach to note-taking or memory jogging. This device is not only straightforward to use and easy to customize with plug-ins, but it’s also cheaper than its competitors, at $75. It helped me keep track of stray thoughts, dates, and my long list of personal and work-related to-dos.

I can genuinely say it helped me remember things I would’ve forgotten, and I appreciate its minimal approach more than Apple’s always-on listening, which both comes with its own privacy concerns and is less efficient.

  • “Share the current weather condition,” the card says, “to improve local forecasts.” If you tap it, you’re given options to indicate whether the current temperature is accurate, warmer, or colder than the app says, and what your current conditions are, with options like cloudy, clear, rain showers, strong thunderstorms, and rain showers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Default weather apps are notoriously unreliable, but Google is giving customers a chance to help improve things.

Recent findings suggest that A recent patch to the Pixel Weather app introduced a new “Report current weather” card. If the weather you’re experiencing doesn’t match what the app is saying, you can report the discrepancy.

“Share the current weather condition,” the card says, “to improve local forecasts.” If you tap it, you’re given options to indicate whether the current temperature is accurate, warmer, or colder than the app says, and what your current conditions are, with options like cloudy, clear, rain showers, strong thunderstorms, and rain showers.

The card also reveals what the app right now thinks is happening for you to use as the basis for your report. To find the card, scroll all the way to the bottom of your Pixel Weather app.

Also: Your best Google weather app alternatives (and what I recommend instead).

Google stated that it will use your feedback, device location, and “some diagnostic information” to help improve forecasts. Nothing you report will be associated with your Google account. The app doesn’t explain exactly how Google uses your reports, but I’ve reached out to see if the organization can offer any details.

It has been revealed that as someone who doesn’t put a ton of faith into default weather apps, I see this as a step in the right direction toward regaining some trust. Even if it’s not yet clear how Google will use the information you send, the goal of improving forecasts is an important one.

Also: I switched to MyRadar as my main Android Auto weather app and don’t regret it.

A large part of what makes weather apps unreliable is that they lack human insight, and a computer usually can’t grasp the nuance of a local forecast the way a meteorologist would. Experts have also warned of reduced weather forecast accuracy due to recent NOAA budget cuts.

Sources indicate that the Apple Weather app has a similar feature, so it’s good to see Google catch up. I couldn’t find a feature like this for Samsung or any other native app. One of the most popular third-party apps, Weather Underground, does feature a “Report your local weather” prompt. It also gathers information from hundreds of thousands of connected home weather stations.

This fresh Pixel Weather feature was present on three Pixel phones in my home, so the rollout appears to be widespread.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You might have to wait over a year to get the Samsung Galaxy Watch 10: Samsung will not release any newly introduced Galaxy smartwatch in 2027, South Korea’s ET News reported on Sunday.
  • In an effort to cut costs after two quarters of consecutive losses and amid global RAM shortages, Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Business division will switch from an annual release schedule to a biannual one for its smartwatches, according to ET News.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am not mad at this decision by Samsung.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You might have to wait over a year to get the Samsung Galaxy Watch 10: Samsung will not release any newly introduced Galaxy smartwatch in 2027, South Korea’s ET News reported on Sunday.

In an effort to cut costs after two quarters of consecutive losses and amid global RAM shortages, Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Business division will switch from an annual release schedule to a biannual one for its smartwatches, according to ET News. The switch follows other cost-cutting measures that will reduce production of the tech giant’s midrange smartphone lineup while increasing its premium Galaxy S27 offerings.

Recent findings suggest that I am not mad at this decision by Samsung. Annual smartwatch updates are usually iterative anyway. Take Apple, for example. Its Apple Watch Series 10, released in 2024, had the same chip as the Apple Watch Series 11, released a year later. The most recent Apple Watch, the Apple Watch Series 12, has the same battery life as the Apple Watch Series 11. I’d expect Apple to keep its new sensors, which debuted on the Series 12 and Ultra 4, for its Series 13 or Ultra 5 next year.

Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9, which debuted with a different chip and added a few more hours of battery, had the same bones as the Galaxy Watch 8.

If some of the biggest features on these smartwatches remain the same for a few years, why not change the release schedule to a biannual one?

In a recent development, also: Galaxy Watch 9 vs. Galaxy Watch 8: I’ve compared both models, here’s my advice.

Some of the most substantial updates that arrive on latest devices like the Galaxy Watch 9 or Apple Watch Series 12 normally arrive through software updates, which end up landing on previous watch generations upon launch as well.

By switching from an annual release cycle to a biannual one, Samsung could drum up more excitement and anticipation between introduces, and be able to surprise its customers with more purchase-worthy updates.

Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#33742. Breaking: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1579 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
  • When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
  • Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.

When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.

Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.

Recent findings suggest that “Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”.

In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”.

According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”.

Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output stated, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.

Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.

A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”.

Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.

But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the concerns the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving consumers other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”.

Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse consumers in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.

Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.

But Aten noted the response wasn’t good enough.

“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”.

It has been revealed that around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user remarked that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.

“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”.

In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the problems arose after Meta deployed an revision giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”.

Industry observers note that it seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”.

In a recent development, “We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy concern,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”.

Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.

In a recent development, “If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.

“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.

Since Muse rolled out in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to swiftly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.

But staffers warned Meta that people may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.

In a recent development, meta notes that Muse customers can trust the tech giant to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant noted it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.

According to recent reports, however, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.

On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.

Sources indicate that that testing “indicated the concern described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.

In a recent development, part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”.

It has been revealed that apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already declared changes coming in response to owners complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple remarked.

#33741. Tech Report: The loneliest peptide party in Newly introduced York

Tech Report: The loneliest peptide party in Newly introduced York

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life.
  • On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.﻿.

Photography by Jack Califano / The Verge.

Recent findings suggest that this is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in Upcoming York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.

Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a newly introduced type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The company makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.).

Welcome to a peptide launch party.

Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in Newly introduced York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.

One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no intends, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he said.

The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.

A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.

In a recent development, after 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.

According to recent reports, as it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and said, “Giggles.”.

If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging says. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.

First of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.

In a recent development, for all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.

All that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “crucial cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.

Recent findings suggest that if everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”.

PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.

It has been revealed that another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”.

As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.

In a recent development, and good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow indicates it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.

I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.

Sources indicate that not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in New York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.).

But a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.

Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even announced it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.

In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.

It has been revealed that it’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

#33737. This lightweight Linux distro ditched KDE Plasma – and it’s better than ever

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (956 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

This lightweight Linux distro ditched KDE Plasma – and it’s better than ever

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that kaOS 2026.11 is a free, systemd-free Linux distribution that delivers outstanding desktop performance, even on older computers with as little as 2GB of RAM.
  • With KDE Plasma no longer an option, does the distro still stand up to its previous incarnations?
  • Sources indicate that for those who’ve never heard of Niri, it’s a lightweight tiling window manager that takes a very different approach to managing windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that kaOS 2026.11 is a free, systemd-free Linux distribution that delivers outstanding desktop performance, even on older computers with as little as 2GB of RAM. I recently wrote about KaOS Linux dropping KDE Plasma as its default desktop environment. At that time, KaOS retained KDE Plasma in its repositories, so people could, if they so chose, install the more familiar KDE Plasma DE. In a recent development, however, the KaOS team decided to remove KDE Plasma from the repositories, making the “K” in KaOS no longer necessary.

With KDE Plasma no longer an option, does the distro still stand up to its previous incarnations? Let’s find out.

Sources indicate that for those who’ve never heard of Niri, it’s a lightweight tiling window manager that takes a very different approach to managing windows. Instead of the traditional tiling window manager approach of placing apps in the most logical, convenient location on the display (which can lead to smaller and smaller windows as you open more apps), Niri goes with a never-ending horizontal strip that can be scrolled.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

Sources indicate that that pattern continues as you open more apps, with each succeeding app opening to the right of the previous one. As each app opens, you can drag it to the right or the left (via the title bar) to move the strip along. Find the app you want and use it. Niri presents a very elegant solution to multitasking: It’s simple to use and fast.

But what has changed in KaOS (other than the removal of KDE Plasma from the repositories) since I last reviewed it? This fresh iteration is 2026.11, which was recently released, and the changes are subtle but notable.

The first thing I noticed was that KaOS now uses Noctalia, which is a native Wayland desktop shell. This shell provides the desktop layer for the Wayland compositor, a layer that consists of things like title bars, the launcher, notifications, the lock screen, and wallpaper.

Industry observers note that there was one single reason why KaOS switched to Noctalia (which also informs us as to why the developers dropped KDE Plasma from the repositories). Because KaOS shrugged off systemd as its init system, a newly introduced window shell had to be used. It’s not that the KDE Plasma KWin window manager requires systemd, but since KDE Plasma does use systemd as a manager for KWin, it became a no-brainer.

You also get a ton of settings to play with, so much so that it can be a bit overwhelming.

Noctalia v5 is built directly on Wayland and OpenGL ES, and the end results are far faster and far smoother than what I’d previously experienced with KaOS. To me, that’s the big change because the speed of KaOS 2026.11 blows away the last release I’d tested. Animations are like butter, and there’s zero screen tearing or stuttering as you drag the app strip from side to side. This is macOS-level smoothness, and I’m all for it.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend.

Industry observers note that another change in KaOS 2026.11 is the display manager, which is now greetd (with tuigreet). The greetd display manager integrates with seatd (a seat management daemon for Linux that mediates access to shared devices). In addition to tuigreet (which is a console-based greeter), KaOS also has the option to use noctalia-greeter, which is based on greetd with the addition of the GUI element. The one caveat is that noctalia-greeter is not quite as complete as tuigreet, so use it at your own discretion.

There are also a few new packages that have been added into the mix, including dex (which brings full XDG autostart support for a non-systemd system), kss (a KConfig module application to adjust settings for KDE applications), Zig and libghostty (to enable early testing of KDE Plasma’s new GPU-supported terminal emulator, kwi), and Croeso (the new onboarding app). The android-tools package has been re-added.

Another bit of good news is that KDE apps are still available to install from the KaOS repositories, even without KDE Plasma. I tested this theory by installing KMail, which worked perfectly.

As I mentioned, these changes had to take place as KaOS remains a systemd-free distribution, which doesn’t exactly work well with the latest releases of KDE Plasma. For the users, it matters because KaOS now feels like it belongs on the desktop; it runs incredibly well, feels rock solid, and levels up multitasking with a simple workflow that will have you wondering why no one had thought of it before (thank you, Niri).

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux.

According to recent reports, more than anything (for me), the fresh KaOS runs so smoothly. I’ve used other distros with Niri (such as Pond), and none of them can compete with the performance and smoothness of KaOS. For me, KaOS unseats every lightweight Linux distribution to become the best option for older machines.

To run KaOS, all you need is a 64-bit x86 CPU and 2GB of RAM (4GB being the recommended minimum). That’s chump change in the modern world. To be fair, I installed KaOS on a desktop machine with an Intel Core Ultra 9 CPU and 32GB of RAM, but I have experienced the OS on machines with as little as 3GB of RAM and only two CPU cores, and it still holds up.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a systemd-free Linux distribution with a unique desktop UI and outstanding performance, do not overlook KaOS 2026.11. You can download the ISO for free from the official KaOS download site.

Breaking: Claude can ship code for you now – how to try it (if you dare)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it.
  • It has been revealed that with Claude Ship, confirmed in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said.
  • Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developers are already using Claude Code and other AI-powered coding tools like OpenAI’s Codex in droves, but some still want to check code themselves before pushing it. A fresh feature from Anthropic is banking on more adventurous, agent-first coders being comfortable with handing even that last step off to AI.

It has been revealed that with Claude Ship, confirmed in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward individual developers or companies who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code.

“Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic remarked. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

It has been revealed that the new feature uses two new agents alongside Code Review, which Anthropic released in March for Teams and Enterprise plans. Code Review first collects, organizes, and posts findings to a PR. Then, Anthropic said, the agents, PR Steward and Claude Approvals, guide a PR “through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually.”.

PR Steward can’t approve or merge pull requests, designed instead to participate “on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members.” It also documents what it changed in each push through comments and provides instructions for how to undo it, should developers want to. Throughout the process, developers can give Claude instructions or tell it to stop by commenting @claude.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free – how it went.

As a final step, Claude Approvals references whatever policy the user or team abides by (which developers provide as a repo file), and additional signals developers set, like Code Review findings, before approving changes autonomously if allowed. If not, it will seek out “deeper human sign-off,” Anthropic said.

“It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file,” the release added. Anthropic noted it recommends that most customers enable those additional checks “first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals’ green light.”.

Admins can select which repos the feature runs in and adjust settings as needed.

But Claude Ship isn’t meant for everyone.

Sources indicate that “Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs.

ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz remarked the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective.

Also: Claude Code vs. Codex: Why I use both and how to choose one (if you must).

“But, it does depend on the team’s workflow and the kind of development they’re doing,” he mentioned. “It’s not something for every team and certainly not for every indy developer, but for certain deployment processes, it could shave a ton of time off turnaround, saving money and potentially sending fixes to customers much faster. ‘Tis cool.”.

Ultimately, Gewirtz remarked he has reasons to both trust the tool and be concerned about what it means for younger developers in the workplace.

“Since that workflow is often assigned to less experienced members of the team, it’s likely that Claude would be as accurate, although it’s one more way to shut the junior members out of where they add value to the company and grow their skills to become senior decision makers,” he said.

Developer platforms overall are adapting to the upcoming state of the industry. Entire, a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents.

Individuals with a Pro, Max, or Ultra subscription can use the /ship command now available in Claude Code, meaning “owners won’t notice any significant increase in token usage,” an Anthropic representative explained. Team and Enterprise users can use Claude Ship for Github repos, and it is billed on tokens, so your overall bill may change.

In a recent development, still, that depends on the number of PRs customers are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the latest PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command.

It has been revealed that anthropic added that certain Enterprise organizations “can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming” by Jan. 15, 2027.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard.

As with other Claude features, like the still-to-come Meetings, customers with a zero-data-retention policy and other privacy configurations don’t have access to Claude Ship.

According to recent reports, morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

It has been revealed that nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

In a recent development, the stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

Bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

Industry observers note that that’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

According to recent reports, what makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

Industry observers note that as for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board indicates it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and said the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

According to recent reports, perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers….

1Password states the security breach didn’t compromise its vaults, but didn’t mention how many customers were affected.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Recent findings suggest that 1Password states a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put consumers at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.

Recent findings suggest that the password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

In a recent development, it also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to consumers to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

In a recent development, the password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a upcoming detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company notes it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that people should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

Industry News: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home.
  • Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat.
  • The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.

At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.

“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit remarked. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”.

Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly remarked. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”.

The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.

Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.

The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—stated that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”.

In a recent development, the complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.

“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt noted. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”.

It has been revealed that all the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.

In a recent development, car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, stated his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”.

Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.

Sources indicate that “The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield mentioned. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”.

It has been revealed that the teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.

Sources indicate that in a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.

Industry observers note that the OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.

It has been revealed that they also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG remarked.

Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”.

In a recent development, another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.

Sources indicate that these recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.

“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.

The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.

It has been revealed that BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.

Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.

“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell remarked. “We understand why they want answers.”.

Mitchell mentioned that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.

“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell stated. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”.

Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The Fresh York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”.

“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang remarked.

As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she remarked.

Sources indicate that “I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield mentioned. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”.

Sources indicate that kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”.

As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release stated. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”.

How to remove Copilot AI from Windows 11 completely – in 6 steps

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft continues to tout Copilot and keeps pushing more AI into Windows, believing that everyone is yearning for an “agentic OS.” But many people simply want a cleaner and more reliable platform that hosts their applications and files without all the AI bells and whistles.
  • Industry observers note that yes, Microsoft has heard the cries and complaints and has been making strides toward improving Windows.
  • Industry observers note that like any AI, Copilot can make mistakes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft continues to tout Copilot and keeps pushing more AI into Windows, believing that everyone is yearning for an “agentic OS.” But many people simply want a cleaner and more reliable platform that hosts their applications and files without all the AI bells and whistles.

Industry observers note that yes, Microsoft has heard the cries and complaints and has been making strides toward improving Windows. However, Copilot still maintains a strong, sometimes unwanted, presence.

Industry observers note that like any AI, Copilot can make mistakes. It can provide wrong information, aka hallucinate. It can tap into your private data if you’re not careful. It can also hog up memory and system resources if you use it heavily. For those reasons and more, you may want to disable or remove Copilot from Windows so it no longer gets in your way.

I’ll present this in steps of varying degrees so you can disable and remove Copilot as little or as much as you want.

Recent findings suggest that by default, the Copilot Windows app starts automatically when you launch the OS. So right off the bat, it’s chewing up memory. To remove it from your startup routine but otherwise keep it around, right-click on the taskbar and select Task Manager from the menu. At the Task Manager window, click the icon for Startup apps. Right-click on the entry for Copilot and select Disable from the menu.

Sources indicate that alternatively, go to Settings, select Apps, and then click Startup. Turn off the switch for Copilot.

There is one downside here. If you open Copilot and then close its window, the app remains in memory, again hogging system resources. To actually close the app, you have to right-click on its system tray icon and select Exit.

It has been revealed that if you want to remove the Copilot Windows app, head to Settings, select Apps, and then click Installed Apps. Look for Copilot in the list, click the three-dot icon, and then select Uninstall.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, head to the Windows 11 Start menu and either scroll down the screen or go to the Apps section. Right-click on the entry for Copilot and select Uninstall.

It has been revealed that ahh, but there’s more to do if you want to completely get rid of Copilot. Even if you uninstall it, the app could resurface courtesy of a future Windows Revision.

Sources indicate that to prevent any future installations of Copilot through Windows Revision, you’ll need to turn to Group Policy on your PC. There are two potential changes you can make in Group Policy. To open the tool, press Win+R to display the Run dialog box. In the text field, type gpedit.msc and click OK.

In the Group Policy Editor, first navigate to the following section: User Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Copilot. Open the setting for “Turn off Windows Copilot” and set it to Enabled.

Sources indicate that for the second setting, both Microsoft Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot need to be installed, and the apps must have been automatically installed rather than installed manually. Plus, you can’t have used Copilot in the past 28 days.

Also: 4 Microsoft To Do app alternatives I’d try before it shuts down.

Under that scenario, this setting will remove both versions of Copilot. For this, go to User Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows AI. Open the setting for “Remove Microsoft Copilot App” and set it to Enabled. You can then close the Group Policy Editor.

Windows 11 Home doesn’t come with the Group Policy Editor, so you have to perform a Registry hack if you’re running this version. In the Run window, type regedit to open the Registry Editor. Head to the following key: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows. Right-click in the empty area on the right, go to Fresh, and select Key. Name it WindowsCopilot. With the WindowsCopilot Registry key selected, right-click on the right, go to New, and select DWORD (32-bit) Value. Name the new value TurnOffWindowsCopilot. Double-click the value, set the Value Data to 1, and then click OK.

Another way to remove Copilot is through a PowerShell script. Right-click on the Start button and select Terminal (Admin) or Windows PowerShell (Admin) from the menu. At the PowerShell prompt, type the following string: Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name “Microsoft.Copilot” | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers. Then type this string: Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers “Copilot” | Remove-AppxPackage -AllUsers. Close the PowerShell window and then reboot your PC. Check the Start menu, and you should find that Copilot has been removed.

Even with Copilot gone, certain AI components and hooks remain in Windows. You can remove them, but the process typically involves more Group Policy changes and Registry edits. However, there are some third-party Windows utilities you can use to handle the process.

One tool, O&O ShutUp10, lets you disable or remove a variety of features and settings in Windows. One option focuses on AI with the ability to disable the Copilot Recall feature, erase any screenshots created by Recall, and completely remove Copilot. Just launch the program, select the tab for AI, and choose the settings you wish to disable or remove.

It has been revealed that another tool, Win11Debloat, can also remove Copilot and its components. A free open-source app, Win11Debloat is available directly on its GitHub page.

After downloading the software, run the Run.bat file as an administrator to launch the program in a PowerShell window. On the main screen, click the Custom Setup button. Check the box to only show installed apps. You may see both Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot. If so, click Next. In the AI section, check any or all of the settings to disable certain AI features. Click Next.

By default, Win11Debloat will back up your Registry and create a system restore point before applying the changes you made. Click Apply Changes to proceed, and then close the program. Restart your PC, and you should find that Copilot and any other AI features you disabled are now gone.

Nothing’s CMF Speaker M review: A $109 Bluetooth speaker that demonstrates up Bose and Sony

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nothing’s budget sub-brand, CMF, just keeps getting better and better, proving that budget tech doesn’t have to be visually unappealing, featureless, or uncool.
  • Also: 3 ways I put my Bluetooth speaker to work during a power outage.
  • Recent findings suggest that I kept two Speaker Ms on my desk for two weeks, and I’m impressed with their performance, even though the modularity aspect is half-baked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing’s budget sub-brand, CMF, just keeps getting better and better, proving that budget tech doesn’t have to be visually unappealing, featureless, or uncool. At $109 a pop (or $79 when on sale), the CMF Speaker M is feature-forward, easily competitive with speakers from more expensive brands, and oddly satisfying to look at.

Also: 3 ways I put my Bluetooth speaker to work during a power outage.

Recent findings suggest that I kept two Speaker Ms on my desk for two weeks, and I’m impressed with their performance, even though the modularity aspect is half-baked. Still, if you like speakers that resemble old-timey milk cartons or look like something out of a 2D cartoon, you’ll like the Speaker M.

In a recent development, have you ever seen gadgets in a cartoon and wished you could use them in real life? That’s how the Speaker M feels to me. Its design is quirky, with a silhouette that mimics a milk carton, vibrant primary colors, circular cutouts for the speaker housings, and an interactive multifunction button reminiscent of a game controller.

The design is cute, fun, and interesting, and it’s a fresh take on Bluetooth speakers, which all tend to look like iterative versions of each other. The Speaker M (and the smaller Speaker S) also features modularity with removable faceplates for customization, though CMF doesn’t yet sell ready-made replacements. For the especially individualistic, you can 3D-print custom faceplates.

In a recent development, I’m not a fan of modularity solely for aesthetic purposes; I stand by my conviction that modular audio products should also offer additional functionality when parts are swapped. I’ve seen it plenty of times — Dyson’s OnTrac headphones have swappable earcups; Fender’s Mix has the same, and now CMF does, too, though it’s an interesting concept to introduce to Bluetooth speakers.

My point is that changing the device’s look alone isn’t a compelling enough reason to buy additional parts.

Beats’ 360 headphones are the best implementation of modularity, with swappable ear pads that not only promote individuality and customization but also serve their own purposes. Changing the earcups changes the headphones’ look and purpose.

Still, the Speaker M has a solid skill set, with Auracast, lossless audio via USB-C, NFC tap-to-pair, and enough physical controls to render your phone unnecessary when the speaker is powered on.

In the Nothing X app, you can play around with the speaker’s soundstage, equalizer, and connectivity. Stereo Mode lets you connect to two speakers and listen in a left/right channel configuration; Night Mode aims to preserve fidelity at low volume; and Low Lag Mode is self-explanatory.

Auracast was very simple and reliable. The Speaker M has an Auracast button on the back; start a stream, press the button, and that’s that.

It has been revealed that I automatically assign major brownie points to any Auracast-enabled device that bypasses the need to join a broadcast through the device’s native Bluetooth settings. Apple isn’t too keen on Auracast (yet … a girl can dream), so whenever the feature resides in the audio device’s settings, I’m already a fan.

Also: I let ChatGPT run my 7 Sonos speakers – and multi-step commands were the best part.

Industry observers note that on to sound. The Speaker M features a 70mm woofer and a 16mm tweeter. Clarity isn’t an issue whatsoever; vocals are clear, and mid-to-high instrumentals are front and center. From Playboi Carti’s “Ahh Yeah” and Trina’s “Told Ya’ll” to Phil Collins’ “Take Me Home” and George Michael’s “Fastlove, Pt. 1,” it’s easy to hear most parts of a track clearly.

However, the Speaker M’s bass performance leaves much to be desired, and even with the volume maxed out, there’s a noticeable absence of deep-reaching frequencies. This problem becomes especially apparent when listening to an Auracast stream, as any changes I made to the equalizer were reverted.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of the Auracast pairing, putting two Speaker Ms on my desk created the ultimate workday listening experience. Though the speakers weren’t paired in a left/right channel configuration, placing one speaker to my left and the other to my right created a center-channel illusion.

I love a deep, punchy bass response, like the one I get from the Bose SoundLink Plus, but the SoundLink Plus’ four passive radiators shake and rattle my desk trinkets.

The Speaker M promises 18 hours of playtime, but I would expect a few more hours on top of that. There’s also no 3.5mm jack, but CMF hopes you’ll just use the USB-C port. If you want to take the Speaker M on outdoor adventures, it has an IP68 durability rating, meaning it’s dustproof and waterproof.

Recent findings suggest that the CMF Speaker M is full of tricks, from useful audio modes and easily translated physical controls to a playful, fresh design. The Speaker M sounds great, and with some tweaking to the bass, you can get a little more of the depth that it lacks out of the box. It won’t match up to what you can get from Bose, Sony, or JBL, but we are talking about a budget brand.

The Speaker M has more features than Bose’s cheapest speaker, the $129 SoundLink Micro, and a more inspiring design than JBL’s $100 Grip and Sony’s $140 Ult Field 1. If versatility and individuality are top of mind, go with CMF.

The Speaker M proves that budget products don’t have to be boring, flat, or devoid of up-to-date technologies. With Auracast on deck, the Speaker M automatically opens itself up to connecting with an unlimited number of other Auracast-enabled speakers; its design is interesting, and its USB-C audio makes it useful for creators and enjoyers alike.

Recent findings suggest that there aren’t any ecosystem barriers keeping the Speaker M from being a full-featured speaker for anyone, regardless of their choice of device manufacturer, which is always a plus in my book. On top of that, most other brands would charge a premium of around $150 or more for all of the features the Speaker M offers.
